lmsArticle.title: High-Level Design: Scaling a Concert Ticket Booking System under Flash Load
lmsArticle.subtitle: Design a scalable concert ticket booking system that handles massive traffic surges and prevents double-booking.
lmsArticle.excerpt: Designing a high-scale ticket booking system requires balancing high read traffic (seat map lookups) with extreme write concurrency (seat lock attempts) during popular concert drops. We achieve this using Redis-based temporary ticket locks and distributed queues.
lmsArticle.content:
## Scenario context

Designing a high-scale ticket booking system requires balancing high read traffic (seat map lookups) with extreme write concurrency (seat lock attempts) during popular concert drops. We achieve this using Redis-based temporary ticket locks and distributed queues.

---

Imagine the ticketing drops for a global pop star. Within seconds of going live, a stadium with 50,000 seats receives over 1 million concurrent conne…

This walkthrough focuses on **System Overview & Scale-Based Design Challenge**.

Before making a design choice, clarify:

- Imagine the ticketing drops for a global pop star.
- Within seconds of going live, a stadium with 50,000 seats receives over 1 million concurrent connection requests.
- If the system is not designed to handle this traffic, database locking bottlenecks occur immediately.

**Concepts in play:** system-design-hld-architectures, caching, distributed-locking, event-driven-architecture

## Stage 1 — Core Requirements and Capacity Estimation

- To establish a clear design scope, we define our requirements and estimate the system capacity.
- Functional Requirements Search & View Event: Users can search for events and view available seats in real-time.
- Reserve Seats: Users can temporarily hold/lock seats for 10 minutes while they enter payment details.
- Confirm Booking: Users complete payment, converting the hold into a confirmed booking.

*Applies **system-design-hld-architectures** to the decision above.*

**Observable outcome:** Confirm Booking: Users complete payment, converting the hold into a confirmed booking.

## Stage 2 — Core Mechanics: API, Schema, and Storage Architecture

- Our system uses separate read and write paths to scale.

*Applies **caching** to the decision above.*

**Observable outcome:** Our system uses separate read and write paths to scale.

## Stage 3 — Practical Interview Execution: 45-Minute Delivery Strategy

- When presenting this design in an interview, manage your time using this schedule: 1.
- Minutes 0-5 (Clarify Requirements): Establish scale expectations (Active users, QPS) and write functional requirements on the whiteboard.
- Minutes 5-15 (High-Level Architecture): Sketch the CDN, Gateway, Read/Write split services, and database layers.
- Minutes 15-30 (Deep Dive): Explain how you prevent double-booking using Redis distributed locks.

*Applies **distributed-locking** to the decision above.*

**Observable outcome:** Minutes 15-30 (Deep Dive): Explain how you prevent double-booking using Redis distributed locks.

## Stage 4 — Apache Kafka: Messaging Configuration

- In high-concurrency booking systems, Apache Kafka is configured with partition keys set to event id .
- This ensures that all transactions for a specific concert drop are processed in order by the same worker instance, preventing write conflicts.
- We configure the topic with replication factor 3 and acks=all to guarantee that message commits are persisted across multiple broker instances, protecting the system against broker failures during drops.

*Applies **event-driven-architecture** to the decision above.*

**Observable outcome:** We configure the topic with replication factor 3 and acks=all to guarantee that message commits are persisted across multiple broker instances, protecting the system against broker failures during drops.

## End-to-end outcome

After working through the stages, you should be able to explain:

- Redis Locks: Use Redis distributed locks for fast, memory-based seat validation.
- Decoupled Paths: Separate the high-traffic seat selection path from the transactional payment system.

## Alternatives considered

The source focuses on one primary design. A second architecture is not compared, so no alternative is invented here.

## Failure and degraded modes

### Lessons Learned: Production Scaling Pitfalls

- **Detection:** Avoid these standard mistakes when deploying booking platforms to production: Setting Long Lock Durations: Keeping seat locks active for too long (e.g., 30 minutes) allows users to tie up inventory w…
- **User or operator impact:** Avoid these standard mistakes when deploying booking platforms to production: Setting Long Lock Durations: Keeping seat locks active for too long (e.g., 30 minutes) allows users to tie up inventory w…

seriesList.name: Architecture Patterns for Production Systems
seriesList.description: High-level design is only half the battle; the other half is surviving production. This series explores the architectural patterns required to build resilient, scalable, and maintainable systems. We dive into the trade-offs of microservices vs. monoliths, event-driven architectures, caching strategies, and data consistency models. Each post focuses on proven patterns that solve common bottlenecks in high-traffic production environments, helping you move from "it works on my machine" to "it works at scale."

seriesList.name: Data Structures and Algorithms
seriesList.description: Master the core of computer science. This series demystifies Data Structures and Algorithms, from Big O to graph theory. Learn to write efficient, scalable code and ace your technical interviews with confidence.

seriesList.name: How It Works: Internals Explained
seriesList.description: Ever wondered what actually happens when you trigger a function, commit a transaction, or deploy a container? This series peels back the layers of abstraction to explore the low-level mechanics of modern technology. From database engines and operating system internals to the hidden plumbing of distributed systems, we dive deep into the source code and architectural designs that make complex software work. No magic, just engineering.

seriesList.name: Low-Level Design Guide
seriesList.description: Good architecture is built on a foundation of solid low-level design. This series is a deep dive into the "micro" side of software engineering—focusing on class design, object-oriented principles (SOLID), and tactical design patterns. We explore how to translate requirements into clean, maintainable code, handle concurrency at the component level, and define clear interfaces. Whether you're preparing for LLD interviews or looking to sharpen your day-to-day coding craftsmanship, this guide provides the blueprints for building modular software.

seriesList.name: Machine Learning Fundamentals
seriesList.description: This series breaks down complex mathematical theories and algorithms into simple, intuitive explanations with practical examples, making AI accessible to everyone from beginners to aspiring data scientists.

seriesList.name: Software Engineering Principles
seriesList.description: Writing code is easy; engineering software that lasts is hard. This series explores the core philosophies and mental models that define professional software development. We go beyond syntax to discuss the timeless principles of modularity, abstraction, testing strategies, and technical debt management. Whether we’re discussing the Zen of Python or the rigors of formal verification, this series provides a high-level perspective on how to think like an engineer, not just a coder.
